title: Nested Loops
learningGoals: explain how an inner loop runs completely for each round of the outer loop
print a grid and a times table with nested `for` loops
use different counter variables for each loop

youtube.title: Nested Loops: Rows and Columns Made Easy | C EP 30
youtube.description: A loop inside a loop sounds scary, but it's just rows of chairs: for every row, go through every seat. We trace nested loops step by step, build a 5×5 times table, and fix the bug where both loops share one variable. 0:00 Challenge answer and hook 0:25 How nested loops work 1:15 Rows and seats, line by line 2:40 A 5×5 times table 3:45 Bug of the Day: same variable in both loops 5:00 Challenge

scenes.onScreen: EP 29 challenge output; then a school hall with 3 rows of 4 chairs
scenes.animation: Chairs drop in row by row, thud SFX
scenes.narration: Last challenge: loop 1 to 30, skip multiples of 4 with continue, and break at the first number above 25 divisible by 7. The output ends at 27, because 28 triggers the break. Now picture the school hall on annual day. Three rows of chairs, four chairs in each row. The teacher checks every chair: row 1, seat 1, 2, 3, 4. Then row 2, seat 1, 2, 3, 4. That's a loop inside a loop.

scenes.onScreen: Clock analogy: hour hand (outer) moves once while minute hand (inner) goes round fully
scenes.animation: Minute hand spins 60 ticks, hour hand clicks once; tick SFX
scenes.narration: A nested loop is simply a loop inside the body of another loop. The outer loop is like the hour hand on a clock. The inner loop is the minute hand. For the hour hand to move once, the minute hand goes all the way round. In code: for every single round of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely, from start to finish. So if the outer loop runs 3 times and the inner runs 4 times, the inner body runs 3 times 4, which is 12 times.

scenes.onScreen: `nested.c` with trackers `row`, `seat` and a counter "prints: n/12"
scenes.animation: Spotlight moves seat by seat; on each `\n` the spotlight drops a row
scenes.narration: [HL 4] Outer loop: for row from 1 to 3. [TRACK row=1] [HL 5] Inner loop: for seat from 1 to 4. [TRACK seat=1] [HL 6] Print R, row, S, seat, and a space. So "R1S1". The inner loop continues: seat 2, "R1S2". [TRACK seat=2] Seat 3, seat 4. [TRACK seat=4] Now seat becomes 5, the inner check fails, and the inner loop is done. [HL 8] We print a newline, so the cursor goes to the next line. That ends one round of the outer loop. Now row becomes 2. [TRACK row=2] And here's the key: the inner loop starts fresh. seat is created again, starting at 1. [TRACK seat=1] So we print R2S1, R2S2, R2S3, R2S4, then a newline. Same again for row 3. When row becomes 4, the outer check fails and we're done. Twelve prints in total. Inner loop prints across. Outer loop moves down.
Compile and run. Three lines, four seats on each. A perfect grid.

scenes.animation: Cells fill row by row; `%4d` padding shown as dotted boxes
scenes.narration: Nested loops can build tables. [HL 4] Outer loop i from 1 to 5. [HL 5] Inner loop j from 1 to 5. [HL 6] printf percent 4 d, and i times j. Percent 4 d means: print this number using at least 4 character spaces, padded on the left. So every number lines up in neat columns, whether it's 1 or 25. [TRACK i=1 j=1] Row 1: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. [HL 8] Newline. [TRACK i=2] Row 2: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. [TRACK i=5 j=5] And row 5 ends with 25. Twenty-five calculations from five lines of code.

scenes.animation: Xecxec inside a box inside a bigger box, rimshot
scenes.narration: Why are nested loops so good at hide and seek? Because they always look inside every row.

scenes.onScreen: `nestbug.c` shares `i`: prints only one row; fixed with `j`
scenes.animation: Butter frame; single `i` tracker jumps to 5 and the outer check fails (Tomato); split into `i` and `j` trackers (Mint)
scenes.narration: Today's bug: same variable in both loops. A student declares int i at the top and uses i for both loops. The outer loop is for i from 1 to 3, the inner loop is also for i from 1 to 4. They expect 3 rows of 4 stars. Compile: no error, no warning. Run it: only one row of 4 stars. What happened? The inner loop takes over i. When the inner loop finishes, i is 5. Back in the outer loop, i plus plus makes it 6. Is 6 less than or equal to 3? No. The outer loop quits after one round. The fix: give each loop its own variable. Outer uses i, inner uses j. Now we get 3 rows of 4 stars. Tip: declaring the counter inside the for, like for int j, helps keep loops separate.

scenes.onScreen: "Ask rows and columns, print a grid of #" with sample 3×5
scenes.narration: Your challenge: ask the user for rows and columns, then print a grid of hash symbols with a space after each. For 3 and 5, you get 3 lines of 5 hashes. Next episode we'll use this exact grid to start drawing stars.
Next episode: pattern printing, the famous star triangles every exam loves. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.why: The inner loop leaves `i` at 5, so the outer loop's `i++` makes it 6 and its condition `i <= 3` fails after one row.

shorts.title: 3 Rows, 4 Chairs, 1 Loop Inside Another
shorts.script: Three rows of chairs, four in each row. To check every chair, you go row by row, and inside each row, seat by seat. That's a nested loop: a loop inside a loop. Full episode on Koding Konkani.
shorts.onScreen: ROW BY ROW / SEAT BY SEAT
shorts.caption: Nested loops are just chairs in a hall.

shorts.title: Nested Loops in 30 Seconds
shorts.script: Nested loops work like a clock. The minute hand goes all the way round for every single move of the hour hand. In C, the inner loop runs completely for each round of the outer loop. Outer 3, inner 4: the inner body runs 12 times. Inner prints across, outer moves down.
shorts.caption: The clock trick for nested loops.

shorts.title: Why Did My Grid Print Only One Row?
shorts.script: Expected 3 rows of stars. Got one. The bug: both loops use i. The inner loop pushes i to 5, then the outer loop adds one, 6, and quits. Give the inner loop its own variable, j, and all 3 rows appear.
shorts.onScreen: ONLY 1 ROW? / SAME i TWICE / USE j
shorts.caption: One variable, two loops, zero luck.

shorts.title: Pun: Hide and Seek
shorts.hook: Xecxec peeking out of a box in a box
shorts.script: Why are nested loops so good at hide and seek? Because they always look inside every row.
shorts.caption: You can't hide from a nested loop.

shorts.title: How Many Stars?
shorts.script: Outer loop runs 5 times. Inner loop runs 5 times. The inner body prints one star. How many stars in total? 25. Five times five.
shorts.caption: Quick maths, nested style.
